extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students interested in Henri Bergson, philosophy, and theories of humor
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts Bergson's philosophical criteria about laughter and the comic (from his essay Laughter) useful for thinking about what provokes or composes comedy. Focuses on Bergson's claims about the nature, function, and stylistic implications of the comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic = 'something mechanical encrusted on the living'
rubrics_metrics.description: Bergson's central definition of the comic: the comic consists in "something mechanical encrusted on the living" (verbatim phrasing from his essay).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation and examples in the article: people laugh when they perceive an inflexible, mechanical aspect imposed on a living being (habits, automatic acts, stiffness). This notion is used to analyze clowns and comic authors who caricature mechanistic behaviour. Use this as an evaluative lens: scenes, characters, or actions that read as mechanical within living contexts are candidates for eliciting laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as a social corrective
rubrics_metrics.description: Bergson describes laughter as "a corrective evolved to make social life possible."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functionally, laughter punishes or corrects behaviour that fails to adapt to social demands by exposing its mechanical or rigid character. For creators/evaluators: consider whether the comic element highlights social maladaptation and thereby performs corrective/social-regulatory work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion of laughter: failure to adapt / inflexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: People laugh at those who fail to adapt to society's demands if that failure "seems their failure is akin to an inflexible mechanism."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: comedic material often hinges on portraying a character or action as rigid, habitual, or automatic in a context that requires flexibility. Examples cited include caricature of habits and automatic acts; assess whether the humour targets such rigidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter is not a moral criterion and can harm self-esteem
rubrics_metrics.description: Bergson warns that "laughter's criterion of what should be laughed at is not a moral criterion and that it can in fact cause serious damage to a person's self-esteem."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators and creators should be aware that laughter's social-corrective function is not synonymous with moral justification; comedic effect can inflict real harm. Use this as an ethical caveat when producing or critiquing humour that targets individuals or groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technique: caricature of mechanistic human nature (habits, automatic acts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bergson identifies that comics and clowns provoke laughter by caricaturing the "mechanistic nature of humans (habits, automatic acts, etc.)."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a prescriptive/diagnostic technique: exaggerate or isolate habitual, automatic behaviours and present them as mechanical to make them comic. The article treats this as an example of the broader 'mechanical encrusted on the living' principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style guideline: favor images and metaphors; use intuition over abstract concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Bergson "makes frequent use of images and metaphors in his writings in order to avoid the use of concepts," arguing intuition and concrete imagery better approach lived reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to humor/arts: prefer vivid images, metaphors, and immediately graspable scenes over abstract conceptual exposition when aiming for comic immediacy or to convey the lived sense of the ludic. This supports comedic techniques that rely on concrete, sensory detail and intuitive perception rather than abstract explanation.
